cards.q: What is CORS?
cards.a: A protocol that lets a server grant permission for a page on another origin to read its responses. Browsers block cross-origin reads by default under the same-origin policy; CORS is how a server opts out of that block, using response headers that the browser checks.

cards.q: What is an origin?
cards.a: Scheme plus host plus port. All three must match for two URLs to be same-origin. Path and query are irrelevant, and subdomains count as different hosts.

cards.q: Why does CORS exist?
cards.a: Because the browser attaches the user's cookies to requests based on the destination, not on who asked. Without a rule, any website could read your bank or email data as you. The same-origin policy blocks that, and CORS is the controlled exception.

cards.q: Who enforces CORS — the browser or the server?
cards.a: The browser. The server only publishes a permission in response headers. That is why curl, Postman and server-to-server calls are unaffected, and why a CORS error means the browser refused to hand you a response, not that the server refused to answer.

cards.q: What is a preflight request?
cards.a: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before a request that the pre-CORS web could not make — anything other than GET/HEAD/POST, any custom header, or a content type a form could not produce. It asks permission first so the real request's side effects never happen without it.

cards.q: Why does a JSON POST trigger a preflight but a form POST does not?
cards.a: The safelisted content types are exactly the three a form can produce — application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/plain. application/json is not among them, because no HTML element could ever have sent it.

cards.q: How do you fix a CORS error?
cards.a: On the server, not the client. Send Access-Control-Allow-Origin with the calling origin (from an allowlist), handle OPTIONS with Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers, add Allow-Credentials: true and Vary: Origin if cookies are involved. Nothing in the frontend can fix it.

cards.q: Why can't you fix CORS from the frontend?
cards.a: The check is on the response, performed by the browser, using headers only the server can set. The one client-side option, mode: "no-cors", gives you an unreadable opaque response — it silences the error rather than fixing anything.

cards.q: Does CORS prevent CSRF?
cards.a: No. CSRF only needs the request to be sent, and simple requests are sent without any permission. CSRF is prevented by SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, and server-side Origin checks.

cards.q: Why can't you use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials?
cards.a: It would mean any site on the internet may read the response as the logged-in user, which is precisely the attack the same-origin policy exists to stop. Browsers reject the combination outright, so you must name a single origin.

cards.q: Your API works in Postman but the browser shows a CORS error. What is happening?
cards.a: Postman has no origin and does not implement the same-origin policy, so it never checks. The server is responding fine; it just is not granting browser read permission. Reproduce it with curl -i -H "Origin: https://your.app" to see the actual headers.

cards.q: Walk me through what happens, request by request, when a React app on port 5173 calls an API on port 3000 with a JSON POST.
cards.a: They are different origins, and the content type is not safelisted, so the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method: POST and Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type. If the server replies 2xx with matching Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers, the browser then sends the real POST, and checks Allow-Origin again on that response before handing it to my code.

cards.q: Which response headers can JavaScript read cross-origin by default?
cards.a: Seven: Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified, Pragma. Anything else needs Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

cards.q: What is Access-Control-Max-Age for and what value would you set?
cards.a: It caches the preflight so repeated calls skip the extra round trip. I'd set 86400 and know that Chrome caps it at 7200 seconds and Firefox at 86400, so the number I send is an upper bound rather than a promise.

cards.q: Why do you need Vary: Origin?
cards.a: Because once you reflect the origin, the response differs per caller. Without Vary, a CDN or browser cache keyed only on URL will serve one origin's Allow-Origin header to a different origin, producing an intermittent CORS failure that disappears when you bypass the cache.

cards.q: Is Authorization a credential in CORS terms?
cards.a: No. Credentials means cookies, HTTP auth and TLS client certs — things the browser attaches by itself. An Authorization header you set is just a header, so it triggers a preflight and must be listed in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, but it does not need Allow-Credentials.

cards.q: What is the difference between same-origin and same-site?
cards.a: Same-origin is scheme, host and port. Same-site is the registrable domain, so app.example.com and api.example.com are different origins but the same site. CORS uses origin; SameSite cookies use site.

cards.q: How do you allow multiple origins?
cards.a: You cannot list them in the header — it holds one origin. You keep an allowlist server-side, compare the incoming Origin by exact string match, echo it back if it matches, and add Vary: Origin.

cards.q: What does credentials: "include" do, and what must the server do in return?
cards.a: It tells the browser to send cookies on a cross-origin request and to honour Set-Cookie on the response. The server must answer with a specific origin — not * — plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true on both the preflight and the real response.

cards.q: Does CORS apply to WebSockets?
cards.a: No. The handshake carries an Origin header but there is no preflight and no allow header, so the server must validate Origin itself. Otherwise any site can open an authenticated socket with the user's cookies.

cards.q: Where in your middleware chain does CORS go, and why?
cards.a: First, before authentication. The preflight is anonymous by design, so if auth runs first it returns 401 on the OPTIONS and the real request is never sent. The symptom looks like an auth bug and is an ordering bug.

cards.q: What is a simple request?
cards.a: A cross-origin request needing no preflight: method GET, HEAD or POST; no author-set headers beyond the safelist; content type one of the three a form can produce; no stream body; no XHR upload listener. It is defined as "what the web could already do before CORS".

cards.q: How would you configure CORS for a public read-only API?
cards.a: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, no credentials, and expose whatever metadata headers consumers need. No allowlist and no Vary needed, because the response genuinely does not vary by origin.

cards.q: What is JSONP and why is it obsolete?
cards.a: A pre-CORS trick: the server wraps JSON in a function call and the page loads it via <script>, since scripts may cross origins and are executed. It is GET-only, has no real error handling, and executes arbitrary code from the remote server in your page. CORS made it unnecessary in 2014.

cards.q: What is canvas tainting?
cards.a: Drawing a cross-origin image into a canvas makes getImageData and toDataURL throw a SecurityError, because reading pixels would leak private images. Fixed with crossOrigin="anonymous" plus Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the image host.

cards.q: Why does window.onerror sometimes report only "Script error."?
cards.a: The error came from a cross-origin script and the details are withheld. You get them back by adding crossorigin="anonymous" to the script tag and Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the CDN — which is exactly what error monitoring setups require.

cards.q: What are COOP, COEP and CORP?
cards.a: Post-Spectre process-isolation headers. CORP says who may embed a resource; COOP severs the window-opener link with cross-origin documents; COEP requires every cross-origin subresource to opt in. COOP plus COEP make a document cross-origin isolated, which re-enables SharedArrayBuffer.

cards.q: What is Origin: null and should you ever allow it?
cards.a: It comes from sandboxed iframes, file:// pages and some redirects. Never allow it — an attacker can produce it at will by sandboxing your page, so allowing it is equivalent to allowing everyone.

cards.q: What is Private Network Access?
cards.a: A Chrome mechanism adding a preflight when a public page requests a private IP or localhost, with Access-Control-Request-Private-Network and a matching allow header. It exists because public pages attacking home routers and local dev servers is a real attack class.

cards.q: Does CORS apply to Server-Sent Events?
cards.a: Yes, normally — EventSource makes an ordinary HTTP request. The catch is that EventSource cannot set headers, so cross-origin auth must use cookies with withCredentials: true or a query parameter.

cards.q: What was document.domain?
cards.a: A legacy way for two subdomains to declare themselves same-origin. It was unsafe because it opened you to any subdomain, and Chrome disabled it by default in version 115 in July 2023.

cards.q: Production frontend suddenly gets CORS errors on about one request in five. Same code, same config. What do you suspect?
cards.a: A cache serving one origin's Access-Control-Allow-Origin to another, because the server reflects the origin but does not send Vary: Origin. The intermittency is the tell — it tracks cache hits. Confirm by comparing responses through the CDN versus direct to origin.

cards.q: A DELETE endpoint returns 401 in the browser but works in curl with the same token. Where do you look?
cards.a: The preflight. It carries no cookies or headers, so auth middleware running before the CORS handler rejects the OPTIONS with 401 and the real DELETE never goes out. Move CORS ahead of auth.

cards.q: You fixed the server config but the browser still fails. What non-obvious cause?
cards.a: A cached preflight — Chrome can hold the old grant for up to two hours. Hard reload with cache disabled, or test in a fresh profile, before assuming the fix did not work.

cards.q: The console says the response contains multiple Access-Control-Allow-Origin values. What happened?
cards.a: Two layers are both adding the header — typically a reverse proxy and the application. Two individually correct configs combining into a broken response. Pick one owner for CORS and delete the other.

cards.q: CORS headers look perfect but every authenticated call returns 401. Diagnose.
cards.a: The cookie never travelled. Cross-site cookies need SameSite=None; Secure, and the client needs credentials: "include". CORS and SameSite are independent gates; a CORS failure is a console error, a cookie failure is a clean 401.

cards.q: CORS errors appear only on 500 responses. What is the real bug?
cards.a: The 500 is the bug. The error path returns a response outside the CORS middleware, so it lacks the headers, and the browser reports the missing header instead of showing you the status. Check the network tab for the real status first.

cards.q: Adding a request ID header broke every call. Why?
cards.a: The custom header took the requests off the safelist, so they now preflight, and the server does not list the header in Access-Control-Allow-Headers. One header turned zero preflights into one per call plus a new failure mode.

cards.q: The preflight fails with a 301. Why, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: Browsers do not follow redirects on a preflight. Something is redirecting — usually a trailing-slash or http-to-https rule. Fix the URL the client calls, or stop redirecting that path; no CORS header will help.

cards.q: A chart export button throws SecurityError in production only. Cause?
cards.a: Canvas tainting — in production a logo or tile comes from a CDN on another origin. Set crossOrigin="anonymous" on the image and make the CDN send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

cards.q: Your frontend cannot read the X-Total-Count header it needs for pagination, though it is visible in DevTools. Fix?
cards.a: Add Access-Control-Expose-Headers: X-Total-Count on the server. Only seven safelisted response headers are readable cross-origin by default.

cards.q: A teammate suggests installing a browser extension to disable CORS. Response?
cards.a: It hides the symptom on one machine while the product stays broken for every user, and it makes that browser unsafe for normal browsing. Use a dev-server proxy instead, which reproduces the production shape rather than removing the check.

cards.q: Preview deployments on Vercel each get a new URL and all fail CORS. How do you handle it?
cards.a: An exact-match allowlist cannot cover generated hostnames. Either add an anchored pattern for the preview domain — carefully anchored, so evil-vercel.app does not match — or proxy the API through the same deployment so previews are same-origin.

cards.q: Same-origin deployment versus separate API origin — how do you decide?
cards.a: Same-origin when there is one frontend and one backend: no CORS, no preflight latency, cookies stay Lax and HttpOnly. Separate origins when many independent clients consume the API, when the frontend is static on a CDN, when teams deploy independently, or when it is a public API.

cards.q: Cookies versus bearer tokens for a cross-origin SPA — CORS implications?
cards.a: Cookies need Allow-Credentials, ban the wildcard, force origin reflection, and depend on SameSite=None; Secure and third-party cookie policy. A bearer token is just a header — simpler CORS, no cookie policy risk — but it lives in the browser where script can reach it, so XSS becomes more costly.

cards.q: Wildcard versus allowlist — when is each right?
cards.a: Wildcard for public, unauthenticated, non-secret resources; it is genuinely correct there and lets caches work with no Vary. Allowlist for anything user-specific or credentialed, where the wildcard is either rejected by the browser or a real vulnerability if reflected.

cards.q: Dev-server proxy versus permissive CORS in development?
cards.a: Proxy. Permissive dev CORS means the real config is never written until staging, and it trains people to reach for *. A proxy makes dev match the shape of a same-origin production, or at least defers the real config to one deliberate place.

cards.q: High Max-Age versus low — what is the trade?
cards.a: High reduces round trips; low means config changes take effect quickly. Since browsers cap it at two hours (Chrome) or a day (Firefox), the real cost of a high value is a stale grant during a config rollout, which is worth planning around during deploys.

cards.q: Exposing a header versus putting the value in the body?
cards.a: The body works identically same-origin and cross-origin, survives proxies that strip headers, and types cleanly. Headers are right when the value is genuinely metadata about the response, like rate-limit budget, that a generic client should read without parsing the body.

cards.q: Should an internal API rely on CORS to restrict access?
cards.a: No — it restricts nothing outside a browser. Use network controls, authentication and authorization. CORS on an internal API is worth configuring only to protect users' browser sessions, never as the access boundary.

cards.q: How does CORS apply to qbank?
cards.a: qbank is a Fastify API. Any browser frontend on a different origin — a local dev server on another port, or a deployed app on another domain — needs @fastify/cors registered before routes, with an explicit origin allowlist rather than a wildcard, credentials enabled if sessions are cookie-based, and Authorization named in the allowed headers since bearer tokens always force a preflight. I have not yet written that config deliberately, which is exactly what this topic's project is for.

cards.q: Your API streams LLM responses. What does that mean for CORS?
cards.a: If it streams over SSE, EventSource is a normal CORS request but cannot set an Authorization header, so auth has to be a cookie with withCredentials or a query parameter. If it streams over fetch with a body reader, headers work normally, but the JSON content type means every call preflights.

cards.q: What would you change about a project that had CORS wide open?
cards.a: Replace the wildcard with an environment-configured allowlist checked by exact match, add Vary: Origin, enumerate allowed and exposed headers instead of using *, verify CORS middleware runs before auth so preflights are not rejected, and confirm exactly one layer sets the headers.

cards.q: Have you ever debugged a CORS problem? Walk me through it.
cards.a: The honest structure of the answer: state the symptom, then show the method — check for an OPTIONS row in the network tab, read the exact console message since it names the failing check, reproduce with curl -i -H "Origin: ..." to separate server behaviour from browser enforcement, and only then change config. The method is what is being assessed.

cards.q: Why doesn't the browser just block cross-origin requests entirely?
cards.a: Because the web is built on them — every image, script, stylesheet, font and form crosses origins. Blocking sends would break everything ever written. Blocking reads costs nothing, because reading was never possible before JavaScript existed.

cards.q: Why is the safelist shaped the way it is?
cards.a: It enumerates what the pre-JavaScript web could already do — three methods, a few headers, three form encodings. Nothing on it is new capability, so nothing on it needs new permission. Everything off it is genuinely new and must be asked about first.

cards.q: Why is the preflight anonymous?
cards.a: It is a question about permission, not a request for data, so sending the user's credentials would leak them to a server that has not yet been granted anything. The cost is that auth middleware must not sit in front of it.

cards.q: Why is a CORS error so uninformative to JavaScript?
cards.a: Because a detailed error is itself an information leak: a script could distinguish "blocked" from "host does not exist" and map internal networks by error type and timing. The vagueness is deliberate; the detail goes to the console, where only a human sees it.

cards.q: Why are most response headers hidden cross-origin?
cards.a: Same default-deny principle one level in. Headers carry application data — totals, IDs, rate limits, tokens — that a server author never considered exposing. Denying by default means nothing leaks unless someone opts in with Expose-Headers.

cards.q: Why did SameSite have to be added when CORS already existed?
cards.a: CORS governs reading; CSRF only needs sending, which CORS never restricted. Fixing the send side required changing cookies themselves, which is what SameSite does — and Chrome made Lax the default in February 2020.

cards.q: Trace exactly what the browser checks on a credentialed preflighted request.
cards.a: On the OPTIONS: 2xx status, Allow-Origin equal to the origin (not *), Allow-Credentials: true, requested method present in Allow-Methods, every requested header present in Allow-Headers. On the real response: Allow-Origin equal to the origin again, and Allow-Credentials: true again. Then it applies Expose-Headers before handing the response to script.

cards.q: Why does Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * not cover Authorization?
cards.a: The Fetch spec special-cases it, because Authorization is high-value enough that a blanket wildcard should not silently permit it. You must name it explicitly, and under credentials * means the literal asterisk anyway.

cards.q: How is the preflight cache keyed?
cards.a: By origin, URL, method and header set, with the browser's own cap on the lifetime. A grant for POST /orders does not cover DELETE /orders/42, which is why a chatty REST API can pay many preflights despite a high Max-Age.

cards.q: How would you review a CORS implementation for vulnerabilities?
cards.a: Look for reflection without an allowlist, substring or unanchored regex matching, Origin: null in the allowlist, wildcard combined with credentials via reflection, missing Vary: Origin, and whether the endpoints behind it return user-specific data at all — that last one determines the severity.

cards.q: Why is endsWith("example.com") a vulnerability?
cards.a: It matches https://evil-example.com and https://notexample.com. Anchored full-string comparison is the only safe form; if a subdomain wildcard is needed, the pattern must be anchored at both ends with the scheme fixed and no dots allowed in the label.

cards.q: What performance cost does CORS add and how do you measure it?
cards.a: One extra round trip per uncached preflight. Measure it in the network waterfall as the OPTIONS row's duration, count how many appear per page load, and reduce it with Access-Control-Max-Age, fewer distinct URL/method combinations, or by eliminating the cross-origin split.

cards.q: Is Origin ever trustworthy for authorization?
cards.a: Only as evidence about a browser, since browsers forbid script from setting it. Any other client forges it freely. It is useful to reject state-changing requests from unexpected origins as defence in depth, never to grant access.

cards.q: Write a production-grade Express CORS config for a cookie-authenticated API.
cards.a: app.use(cors({ origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, !o || ALLOWED.has(o)), credentials: true, methods: ["GET","POST","PUT","PATCH","DELETE"], allowedHeaders: ["Content-Type","Authorization"], exposedHeaders: ["X-Total-Count"], maxAge: 86400 })) mounted before auth, with ALLOWED built from an environment variable.

cards.q: Same thing in Fastify.
cards.a: await app.register(import("@fastify/cors"), { origin: (origin, cb) => (!origin || ALLOWED.has(origin)) ? cb(null, true) : cb(new Error("Not allowed"), false), credentials: true, allowedHeaders: ["Content-Type","Authorization"], exposedHeaders: ["X-Total-Count"], maxAge: 86400 }), registered before routes.

cards.q: Why allow requests with no Origin header in that callback?
cards.a: Same-origin browser requests for GET, health checks, server-to-server calls and curl all send none. Rejecting them breaks your own infrastructure while providing no security, since a real attacker's page always sends an origin.

cards.q: What is the nginx add_header pitfall?
cards.a: Headers in a nested block replace inherited ones rather than adding, and without the always flag they apply only to 2xx and 3xx — so error responses lose their CORS headers, and a 500 surfaces as a confusing CORS message.

cards.q: How do you handle preflights in a hand-written nginx config?
cards.a: Intercept if ($request_method = OPTIONS), add Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers and Max-Age with always, and return 204 before proxying — otherwise the OPTIONS reaches a backend that may 404 or 405 it.

cards.q: Where should the allowlist live?
cards.a: In configuration, as an environment variable of comma-separated origins, so staging, preview and production differ without a code change and nobody is tempted to widen it in code.

cards.q: What does mode: "no-cors" actually give you?
cards.a: An opaque response: type: "opaque", status: 0, no headers, unreadable body, no preflight sent. It is useful for fire-and-forget beacons or filling a cache, and it is never a fix for a CORS error.

cards.q: A POST with Content-Type: text/plain carrying JSON — what are the consequences?
cards.a: It is a simple request, so no preflight — which some people use to save a round trip. But it also means an API parsing text/plain as JSON has re-opened itself to CSRF, since an attacker's form can produce that content type.

cards.q: Does a cross-origin redirect affect CORS?
cards.a: Yes. The CORS check applies at each hop, and after a cross-origin redirect the Origin may become null. Preflights do not follow redirects at all.

cards.q: Can you read a cross-origin stylesheet's rules?
cards.a: No — document.styleSheets[i].cssRules throws a SecurityError for a cross-origin sheet without CORS. The styles apply; the text is not readable. Same display-without-read rule as images.

cards.q: Why do cross-origin fonts require CORS when images do not?
cards.a: Firefox has always enforced it for @font-face, historically to respect font licensing and hotlinking concerns. It is why every font CDN sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, and why a missing header shows up as a silent fallback to a system font.

cards.q: Do ES modules behave differently from classic scripts?
cards.a: Yes. <script type="module"> is always a CORS fetch, so a cross-origin module without the header does not load. Classic scripts are not, which is exactly why JSONP was ever possible.

cards.q: Cookies ignore ports but origins do not. What breaks because of that?
cards.a: On localhost, two dev servers on different ports are different origins for CORS but share cookies. You can end up authenticated on a port you never logged into, and confused about which gate is failing.

cards.q: Why does navigator.sendBeacon work where fetch is blocked?
cards.a: It sends in no-cors mode where it can and never needs to read a response — the send side of the asymmetry, which the web has always permitted.

cards.q: What is Subresource Integrity's relationship to CORS?
cards.a: An integrity attribute on a cross-origin resource requires CORS, because the browser must read the bytes to hash them. So SRI on a CDN asset needs crossorigin plus the allow header.
